rationale:
The requirement says the review prompt lists five mechanical changes, which the reviewer makes in the revised text and never phrases as questions. It also says the reviewer does not automatically convert ordinary prose or commented API declarations to RFC keywords, and does not strengthen or weaken what the draft promises.

`tests/authoring_cli.rs#fn[the_review_prompt_lists_the_mechanical_changes]` takes the prompt text between the `**Mechanical changes:**` and `**Design questions:**` headings. It does this through `review_prompt_between`, which panics if either heading is missing. It then asserts with `assert_text` that the section contains each of these phrases:
- "Split a compound requirement".
- "Clarify an obligation whose intent is clear while preserving whether behavior is required, recommended, or permitted".
- "Do not automatically convert ordinary prose or commented API declarations to RFC keywords, or strengthen or weaken what the draft promises".
- "Fix wording whose resolution is obvious: vague terms, inconsistent terms, an ambiguity with one sensible reading".
- "Add an `{example}` where a concrete case pins an obligation down".
- "Update other requirements a change makes stale".

A second assertion on the same section checks for "make them yourself in the revised text, and never phrase them as questions".

Together these cover every obligation in the text: the five bullets, the no-questions rule, the preservation of required, recommended or permitted status, and the rule against automatic keyword conversion or strengthening and weakening. `assert_text` fails with a message naming any missing phrase. The assertions are scoped to the right section, so phrases found elsewhere in the prompt cannot satisfy them. The prompt text is the only observable output, so substring checks on it are appropriate. I found no uncovered obligation or marking gap.

text: The review prompt treats the following as mechanical changes, which the reviewer
makes in the revised text and never phrases as questions:
- clarifying an obligation whose intent is clear while preserving whether the
behavior is required, recommended, or permitted;
- rewording vague or inconsistent terms, or an ambiguity, where only one resolution is sensible;
- adding an `{example}` that pins an obligation down;
- updating other requirements that a change makes stale.
Ordinary prose and commented API declarations can express obligations. The reviewer
does not automatically convert them to RFC keywords or strengthen or weaken
